content: The study included both White and Black adults aged 45 years or older with hypertension (HTN). Antihypertensive treatment was determined to be cost-effective across all groups, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) exceeding $10,000. In an economic analysis funded by Novartis, data from the AIPRI study were used to model transition probabilities for patients with chronic kidney disease treated with benazepril. However, the rationale for selecting other input sources was unclear. Benazepril was found to be the dominant treatment over a 7-year time horizon. In Ghana, Gad and colleagues conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis using a state transition model with six health states, one-year cycle lengths, and a lifetime horizon. They compared the cost-effectiveness of various antihypertensive drug classes, including ACE inhibitors (ACEi), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), beta-blockers (BBs), calcium channel blockers (CCBs), thiazide-like diuretics, and no intervention. All drug classes were more effective than no intervention, with thiazide diuretics being the most cost-effective at a cost of GHS 276 per disability-adjusted life year (DALY). CCBs were more effective but more expensive, while ACEi, ARBs, and BBs were less effective than thiazide diuretics. These findings were consistent in sensitivity analyses. Ekwunife and colleagues performed a cost-utility analysis of antihypertensive medications in Nigeria using a Markov model with six health states, one-year cycle lengths, and a 30-year time horizon. Patients were stratified by cardiovascular risk. Probabilistic sensitivity analyses showed that thiazide diuretics were the most cost-effective option across all cardiovascular risk groups, followed by CCBs, at a willingness-to-pay threshold of at least $2,000 per QALY. The results were robust to parameter changes. An industry-sponsored cost-utility analysis by Solvay Pharmaceuticals compared eprosartan with enalapril and nitrendipine, finding eprosartan to be cost-effective at a willingness-to-pay threshold of €30,000. Another industry-funded study by Pfizer in Taiwan compared amlodipine and valsartan using a Markov model with a five-year time horizon. This study did not include a systematic literature review for its inputs but found amlodipine to be the dominant treatment, with results robust in sensitivity analyses. A non-industry-funded study in Poland compared ACE inhibitors and ARBs, finding that ACE inhibitors provided better outcomes. Switching from ARBs to ACE inhibitors resulted in an annual gain of 830 QALYs and 1,018 life-years for the Polish population. An economic evaluation sponsored by Daiichi-Sankyo in China used a well-designed Markov model with five health states and a 20-year time horizon. The study found that a single-pill combination of olmesartan/amlodipine was dominant compared to multiple-pill combinations of olmesartan and amlodipine or valsartan/amlodipine. Similarly, in Poland, a single-pill combination of indapamide and amlodipine was found to be cost-saving compared to multiple-pill therapies. These findings were consistent in sensitivity analyses. Lung et al. evaluated the cost-effectiveness of a triple-pill strategy (amlodipine, telmisartan, and chlorthalidone) compared to usual care using data from the TRIUMPH trial. The model, with a 10-year time horizon, showed robust findings despite the lack of a systematic review for input selection. The cost per DALY averted was $79 over 10 years. In low-income countries, medications like beta-blockers, loop diuretics, and statins may be available in some community health systems but are often not covered by health insurance at the commune level. Patients face challenges such as inconsistent prescribing practices and short prescription durations, which increase treatment costs, reduce compliance, and hinder hypertension control. Research on optimal antihypertensive treatments for Black patients is limited. Subgroup analyses and cohort studies suggest that Black patients may experience higher rates of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events with ACEi or ARB monotherapy compared to other antihypertensives. Increasing treatment adherence among Black adults could help address racial disparities in care. African Americans may face unique barriers to hypertension management, including impaired access to healthcare and education, distrust of the healthcare system, and alternative beliefs about hypertension. These factors may lead to nonadherence or reliance on community-based care. Medication adherence improves with fewer logistical barriers, such as easier access to clinics and health insurance. Simplifying dosing regimens, such as using single-pill combinations, has been shown to improve adherence by 6–20%. However, single-pill combinations may limit dose flexibility and require discontinuation of the entire combination if side effects occur. Economic evaluations consistently show that single-pill combinations are cost-effective and improve adherence. However, the lack of systematic reviews in some studies raises concerns about potential bias in input selection.
